desc:
The arrays a and b are each sorted in non-decreasing order (either may be empty, but not both). Imagine merging them into one sorted sequence of a.length + b.length values, keeping duplicates. Return the k-th value of that merged sequence (1-indexed), without actually building it.

Example: for a = [1, 4, 7], b = [2, 3, 9, 10] the merged sequence is 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, 10, so k = 4 gives 4. Aim for O(log(min(a.length, b.length))) time.
constraints: Both arrays are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Merging with two pointers takes O(k). To be faster you must discard many elements at once.
The k smallest values consist of some prefix of a with i elements and a prefix of b with k - i elements. Only i is unknown.

A split is right when the last taken element of each array is not larger than the first untaken element of the other. If a[i] < b[k - i - 1], then a[i] must also be among the k smallest, so i is too small. Binary search i; the answer is the larger of the two last taken elements.
editorial: Choose how many of the k smallest values come from a; call it i, so j = k - i come from b. The valid range is max(0, k - |b|) ≤ i ≤ min(k, |a|). The split is correct exactly when a[i-1] ≤ b[j] and b[j-1] ≤ a[i] (missing elements count as infinity or minus infinity).

If a[i] < b[j-1], then a[i] is smaller than a value we already took from b, so it belongs to the k smallest and we must take more from a: move the lower bound to i + 1. Otherwise the split is not too small and the upper bound moves to i. Swapping the arrays first so that a is the shorter one keeps the search to O(log min(|a|, |b|)).

When the search ends the k smallest values are a[0..i-1] and b[0..j-1], so the k-th is the larger of a[i-1] and b[j-1] (ignoring a side that contributes nothing). This is the building block of the classic median of two sorted arrays problem. Space is O(1).
